article_title: User Interface Design for E-Learning Software
citation: Behnam Faghih, Mohammad Reza Azadehfar, S. D. Katebi. (2013). User Interface Design for E-Learning Software. The International Journal of Soft Computing and Software Engineering [JSCSE], Vol. 3, No. 3.
title: UIDEL: user interface design for e-learning as the intersection of UI design principles and learning psychology
description: The article proposes that designing the user interface of educational software requires combining conventional UID principles with principles and concepts of learning. It frames UI as "the point of interaction between user and educational body" and argues that educational aims may fail even with good content if this correlation is unsuccessful. The framework organizes its analysis around stimulus/motivation, working memory, multimedia presentation, and availability as UI-relevant learning factors.
requirements: Design must begin with an understanding of the intended users, including profiles of their age, sex, physical abilities, education, cultural or ethnic background, motivation, goals and personality
constraints: The article states it focuses only on psychological issues of user interface design among the many disciplines involved in e-learning
examples: The authors illustrate the framework through educational software they built, showing how UI can improve learning, motivation, and time efficiency
key_sources: Behnam Faghih, Mohammad Reza Azadehfar, S. D. Katebi. (2013). User Interface Design for E-Learning Software. The International Journal of Soft Computing and Software Engineering [JSCSE], Vol. 3, No. 3. https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.6365

article_title: Integrating a Computational Perspective in Physics Courses
citation: Marcos Daniel Caballero and Morten Hjorth-Jensen. (2018). Integrating a Computational Perspective in Physics Courses. https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08871v1
title: University of Oslo Computing in Science Education project and its synchronized physics bachelor program
description: The Computing in Science Education project at the University of Oslo, later the Center for Computing in Science Education (a Center of Excellence in Education), has since 2003 introduced computing across disciplines in a synchronized way. Its elements include "a compulsory programming course with a strong mathematical flavour", coordination of computational exercises in most undergraduate courses, staff development support, and new textbooks. The article lists the program's semester-by-semester course layout in table 1.1.
requirements: Willingness of teachers to prioritize teaching reforms and course transformations
target_learners: undergraduate physics students at the University of Oslo
target_learning_goals: computing competencies integrated into physics and mathematics courses
examples: Table 1.1 shows the Oslo physics bachelor's program, with IN1900 Intro to Programming and MAT-INF1100 Modeling and Computations in the first semester alongside MAT1100 Calculus
key_sources: Marcos Daniel Caballero and Morten Hjorth-Jensen. (2018). Integrating a Computational Perspective in Physics Courses. https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08871

article_title: Physics Computational Literacy: Programming, modeling and collaboration at the journeyman level
citation: Karl Henrik Fredly, Tor Ole B. Odden, and Benjamin M. Zwickl. (2026). Physics computational literacy: Programming, modeling, and collaboration at the journeyman level. Physical Review Physics Education Research 22, 010103. https://doi.org/10.1103/6fny-yzyb
title: University of Oslo computational physics curriculum: computation integrated from the first semester through project-based courses and computational essays
description: The physics curriculum at the University of Oslo integrates computation throughout the degree. The article states that "The computational elements of the curriculum are structured as follows: at the beginning of their bachelor's studies, students are taught the basics of calculus, mechanics, programming, and computational modeling." First-semester courses give a Python baseline; later courses add computational essays, an astronomy course with a large optional project, a C++ computational physics course with five large projects, and a project-based machine learning course where students implement models from scratch. Group work on projects adds collaboration challenges.
requirements: Later courses assume a degree of competence with computation established by the first-semester programming and computational modeling courses.
constraints: The study population is specific to this Norwegian program; most students enter with some high-school programming experience since 2020.
target_learning_goals: numerical methods such as Runge-Kutta and Markov chain Monte Carlo
examples: In third-semester electromagnetism and fourth-semester waves and oscillations, students write computational essays modeling and exploring a physics phenomenon in a computational notebook environment.
key_sources: Karl Henrik Fredly, Tor Ole B. Odden, and Benjamin M. Zwickl. (2026). Physics computational literacy: Programming, modeling, and collaboration at the journeyman level. Physical Review Physics Education Research 22, 010103. https://doi.org/10.1103/6fny-yzyb

article_title: Willingness to volunteer and readiness to practice of undergraduate medical students during the COVID-19 pandemic: a cross-sectional survey in Indonesia.
citation: Lazarus Gilbert, Findyartini Ardi, Putera Azis Muhammad, Gamalliel Nico, Nugraha David, Adli Imam, Phowira Jason, Azzahra Lyanna, Ariffandi Bagas, Widyahening Indah Suci. (2021). Willingness to volunteer and readiness to practice of undergraduate medical students during the COVID-19 pandemic: a cross-sectional survey in Indonesia. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02576-0
title: COVID-19 pandemic response massive open online course for medical students (Universitas Indonesia)
description: A massive open online course implemented by an Indonesian medical institution to equip medical students with essential biomedical, clinical, and epidemiologic knowledge on COVID-19. The article reports that "the course also provided basic skills trainings including infection prevention and control, mass education, and risk communication through video lessons and webinar sessions". The article cites evidence that MOOC use during the pandemic has been shown beneficial in strengthening healthcare systems, and that online PPE training produced comparable performances to offline instructor-led training.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students and health profession students
target_learning_goals: COVID-19 biomedical, clinical and epidemiologic knowledge
Risk communication and mass education skills
examples: Delivered through video lessons and webinar sessions by the Medical Education Unit, Faculty of Medicine Universitas Indonesia
